sentences.text: From question to publication with the Aurora: testing two television commercials
This workshop follows one advertising question from the first sentence a client says to the last sentence of a written results and discussion section.

You will plan a test of two television commercials, build it in iMotions Lab 11 point 1, set up the Smart Eye Aurora and calibrate each viewer (a short routine that teaches the tracker that viewer's eyes), measure attention on moving video, test three hypotheses, and write the result for a journal and for a client.
Every section explains why a step exists before it shows how.
Screen based eye tracking records where on a screen a viewer looks, and when.
The Aurora, a slim bar mounted under the lab monitor (Smart Eye, n.d.)
, lights the eyes with infrared light and finds two landmarks in each eye image: the center of the pupil and a small reflection of the light on the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye.
As the eye turns, the pupil moves while the reflection stays nearly still, so the offset between them gives the direction of gaze.
The method is called pupil center corneal reflection (P C C R).
At the lab Aurora's sampling rate of 60 hertz, one gaze sample (one estimate of the point on the screen where the eyes are directed) arrives every 16.67 milliseconds.
Because the screen is fixed and every viewer sees the same frame at the same moment, each sample already has its place on the stimulus.
If you did Workshop 1, notice what is gone: no gaze mapping, the step that projected each wearer's moving scene video onto a photograph of the shelf.
The method shows where and when, not why, and not how much the viewer liked what was seen; attention predicts choice without measuring it.
Commercials make a natural second study because attention is the gate that every other advertising effect passes through.
The brand, the pictures, and the text of an ad compete for the eye, and fixations on the brand feed later memory for it.

When the brand appears affects whether viewers who can avoid a commercial stay with it, and viewers who fast forward keep their eyes near the center of the screen, where brand information can still get through.
The worked example is real material: the iMotions demonstration study "the demo Sony Bravia study" in the lab's Library, built around two Sony Bravia commercials, "Balls" and "Paint".
A simulated data set of 30 viewers carries the numbers.
The Aurora works with either lab computer, because both license keys include the Eye Tracking Screen based module, and its Smart Eye setup is made once for each computer and monitor.
Time needed.
About 4 hours over two sittings: sections 01 to 05 (question, design, build, collect) in the first, 06 to 10 (methods, numbers, analysis, writing) in the second
Equipment.
The Smart Eye Aurora with its mount and U S B cable, the lab monitor, and a lab computer (the laptop or the desktop)
SoftwareiMotions Lab 11 point 1 and the Smart Eye Tracker software, plus R or Excel for section 08
Data files.

The simulated ad test files in the site's data folder (A O I metrics, survey, session log, analysis dot R, the Excel workbook), plus the the demo Sony Bravia study study in the lab Library, opened in class
How to use.
Work top to bottom, answer each quick check, then tick the section
You need a lab computer with iMotions Lab 11 point 1, the Aurora mounted under the lab monitor, and this page.
You do not need Workshop 1 or any experience with iMotions.

The statistics you need are a mean (an average), a standard deviation (how far a typical value sits from the mean), and the idea that a test asks whether a difference is larger than chance would produce.
Every other term is defined where it first appears, and terms with a dotted underline open a one line definition when you tap them.
The help center links open after you sign in through my dot imotions dot com.
At a lab computer, open iMotions in another window to follow the screens in sections 04 and 05.
Nothing in this workshop records into, deletes, or changes the lab's existing studies; open the demo Sony Bravia study only to look.
The one sentence this workshop keeps repeating Decide what you will compare, and how you will measure it, before anyone sits down at the screen.

Two commercials with four measured regions each, and 48 metrics for every region, give hundreds of numbers per viewer; a study without a comparison written in advance will always find something, and that something may be chance.
Say what screen based eye tracking measures and what it cannot, why attention to commercials is worth measuring, and which equipment, software, and files this workshop uses.
From idea to research question
A client rarely arrives with a research question.
A client arrives with a business question, a statement of what the business wants to know or to happen.
Picture a brand manager with two finished commercials for the same television set and money to air one: "Which of our two commercials does more for the product?"
The sentence names a wish and a comparison, but not who will watch, what "does more" means, how it will be measured, or what difference would count.
A research question names the problem the study will answer and signals the type of study needed.
A hypothesis is a testable answer to that question, written with the specific variables that will be measured.

The iMotions design guide asks for both before any data are collected, because writing the expected answer first forces you to say what you would accept as evidence and guards against confirmation bias, the habit of seeing what you expected to see.
The independent variable is what the researcher changes; the dependent variable is what is measured in response.
Here the independent variable is the commercial, with two levels, Balls and Paint.
The lab asks every study to pass through one sentence with four slots: who, sees what, measured how, compared against what.

For the ad test it reads: adult television viewers (who) watch both commercials on the lab monitor, in an order balanced across viewers (sees what), while the Aurora records where they look and a rating slide after each commercial asks how much they liked it (measured how), and each viewer's response to Paint is compared with the same viewer's response to Balls (against what).
If you cannot fill all four slots, you do not yet have a study.
Weak questions fail in three ways, and each can be repaired.
"Which commercial is better?"
is an opinion and too general: better at what, and for whom?
"Does Paint work?"
is missing its what and its how: work at what, shown by which metric, against what?
"What do people look at in commercials?"
has everything as its answer, so nothing can be tested.
The repair names an observable, a measure, and a comparison: "Among the same viewers, is the share of the product shots spent fixating the television set higher in Paint than in Balls?"
The iMotions table below makes the same contrast.
Before choosing measures, separate the three outcomes an ad test can measure, because they are different things and they can disagree.
Attention is where and when the eyes go: whether the viewer fixated the product, how soon the logo was found.
Affect is how the viewer feels about the commercial, here how much it is liked.
Memory is what the viewer can retrieve afterward, such as the brand name in an unaided recall question (asked without showing the brand) at the end of the session.
A commercial can hold the eyes and be disliked, or be enjoyed and leave the brand forgotten.
The eye tracker measures only attention: liking needs the rating slide, and memory needs a question after the commercials.

A large comparison of traditional, eye tracking, physiological, and brain measures as predictors of how ads performed in the market found that the newer measures did not all add the same thing (Venkatraman and colleagues
, 2015), so name the single outcome each measure stands for.
Attention metrics answer where, when, how long, how often, and in what order.
They do not answer why.
A long look at the television set can mean interest, confusion, or admiration for the picture, and the recording looks the same in each case.
Reading a mental state straight off a physiological signal is called reverse inference, and reviews of consumer neuroscience warn against it.
Now the hypotheses, written before any data exist.
They need three more terms.

An area of interest (A O I) is a named region of the stimulus where iMotions computes metrics; on a video it is a dynamic A O I, which follows its element as it moves and counts only while the element is on screen.
A fixation is a period, typically 100 to 300 milliseconds, in which the eyes rest on one spot.
Dwell time ( percent) on the Product TV A O I (the television set in the product shots) is higher in Paint than in Balls.
Dwell time ( percent) is the share of the time the A O I was on screen that the viewer spent fixating inside it.
The time to first fixation (T T F F) on the Brand Logo A O I, the logo on the end card (the closing frame that shows the brand), is shorter in Paint than in Balls.
T T F F is a family of metrics that differ in when the clock starts: T T F F A O I counts from the moment the A O I becomes active, T T F F parent from the start of the commercial, and T T F F max.
gives a viewer who never fixated the A O I the parent's full duration.
H2 uses T T F F A O I, so its clock starts when the logo appears and stops at the first fixation on it.
Liking, rated from 1 to 7 after each commercial, differs between the two commercials.
All three tests in this study are two tailed.
A two tailed test asks whether two means differ in either direction.
A one tailed test looks only in the predicted direction, so it is blind to a difference the other way, and it is defensible only when a difference the other way would be meaningless.
Here it would not be: if Balls held more attention on the product than Paint, or if viewers found the logo sooner in Balls, the client would want to know.
So H1 and H2 each state the direction that the reasoning predicts, and their tests are still two tailed.
H3 states no direction at all, because nothing in the attention argument says which commercial will be liked more (a spectacle can be enjoyed for itself), and its test is two tailed as well.
The directions of H1 and H2 come from reasons.
Pictures capture attention whatever their size, while the brand passes attention on to the other elements, and visual complexity changes an ad's stopping power, its ability to catch and hold the eye.

In this workshop's simulated plan (a plan, not a measurement of the real commercials), the hero element, the balls or the paint, is on screen for 40 seconds in Balls and 32 in Paint, and the product shots for 14 and 20 seconds.
Paint leaves the spectacle less time to compete with the product (H1), and eyes already on the product may find the logo sooner (H2).
Viewers also differ in how far into an ad they go, so averages hide differences between people; a review of eye movements on advertisements summarizes this research.
A hypothesis grounded in a reason is one you can learn from when it fails.
A study run "just to see what we can see" will see something The iMotions design guide puts it plainly: "Biometric measures are granular enough that you can almost always find some result."
The A O I Metrics article lists 48 metrics for every A O I, so four A O I's in two commercials give 384 numbers for every viewer.

Test the 48 metrics on each of the four A O I's for a difference between the commercials and you have run 192 tests; if no real difference existed anywhere, about one test in twenty, roughly ten in all, would still come out significant at the point 0 5 level.
The remedy is to choose one primary metric for each hypothesis before the data exist and to label everything else secondary or exploratory.
Here the primary metrics are Dwell time ( percent) on Product TV for H1, T T F F A O I on Brand Logo for H2, and the 1 to 7 liking rating for H3.
Write them into a dated plan with the hypotheses, the sample size, and the exclusion rule.
Filing that plan before collection is called preregistration, and it lets a reader tell a prediction from a story told afterward.
Section 02 adds the design, section 03 writes the whole plan, and section 08 holds you to it.

Turn a client's business question into a research question and a one sentence comparison, tell attention from affect and memory, write three hypotheses with one primary metric each, and explain why fishing through 48 metrics finds chance.
Designing a within subjects test
A design is the set of decisions that make a comparison fair, and the first is how to assign viewers to conditions.
In a between subjects design each participant experiences one condition; in a within subjects design every participant experiences all conditions.
The iMotions design guide states the trade: between subjects designs need larger samples, while within subjects designs need fewer participants but risk fatigue.
Within subjects also makes each viewer his or her own control, so stable differences between people (some viewers look at products in any commercial) drop out of the comparison.

If you did Workshop 1, you met the other choice: a real shelf could not be reset in front of a shopper, because the first visit taught her where the brand sat, so the shelf study was between subjects.
A screen can show two different commercials in one session.

Within subjects is still wrong when the first condition spoils the second, as with two cuts of one commercial that differ only in the end card: by the second viewing the story is known and the change may be spotted, so that comparison goes back to between subjects.
The price of within subjects is that the first commercial can change how the second is watched.
Carryover is what the first condition leaves behind: knowledge of the brand, the expectation of a product shot, or tiredness.
An order effect is a difference caused by position alone, such as more looking at the product in whichever commercial comes second.
Neither can be removed, but both can be balanced.
Counterbalancing presents each order to equal numbers of viewers so that, in the design guide's words, order effects cancel each other out.
Order A shows Balls first; Order B shows Paint first.
In iMotions each order is a flow, an ordered list of the stimuli a respondent sees.
A study can hold one flow or several, and the study settings assign respondents to flows manually or at random (section 04 builds them).
Manual allocation from a prepared list (A, B, A, B) guarantees equal groups; random allocation keeps the operator's choices out.
The alternative to flows is a test plan, a file listing each respondent and the stimuli he or she will see.
Either way, record the order as a variable, because section 08 checks whether it mattered.
Paired data are powerful.

A viewer who looks at products a lot in one commercial tends to do so in the other; in the simulated data of section 08 a viewer's two product dwell shares correlate at r equals point 4 8 (simulated).
The paired t test works on each viewer's difference, Paint minus Balls, so the stable part of each viewer cancels.
The effect size states how large a difference is in standard units; for paired data it is d z, the mean of the differences divided by their standard deviation.

The more a viewer's two measures move together, the smaller that standard deviation and the larger d z. Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size if it is real; the usual target is 80 percent.
In plain words.

For a large effect, d z equals 0.8, a paired test at two tailed alpha point 0 5 and 80 percent power needs 15 usable viewers; a medium effect, d z equals 0.5, needs 34, and a small one, d z equals 0.3, needs 90.
If you did Workshop 1, compare: the same large effect between subjects needed 26 shoppers per group, and a medium effect between subjects needs 64 per group.
The same calculation in R and G*Power R: power.t.test(delta equals 0.5, sd equals 1, sig.level equals point 0 5, power equals point 8 0, type equals "paired") returns n equals 33.4, rounded up to 34.
G*Power, Means: difference between two dependent means (matched pairs), two tails, d z equals 0.5, alpha point 0 5, power point 8 0: total sample size 34.
G*Power is the program most researchers cite for this.
The conventions 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large were written for differences between groups, so they are only a rough guide for d z.
Three practical rules follow.
The iMotions design guide recommends 20 to 60 people per study condition, and its Static Image Testing template plans 25 per cell.
The lab's convention for a screen study is 25 to 30 usable viewers.
Recruit 20 to 25 percent more than the usable target, because calibration fails for some viewers and some recordings fall below the exclusion rule: 30 usable viewers means scheduling about 36 to 38.

Two commercials are two stimuli, two specific things shown to viewers, not a sample of commercials in general, and a difference between them belongs to everything that differs at once: story, music, product shots, end card.
The result can say that Paint, as made, held more of these viewers' attention on the product than Balls, as made.
It cannot say that spectacle hurts product attention; that needs many commercials analyzed as a sample, called stimulus sampling, with power that depends on the number of stimuli as well as viewers.
Each slide in the session has a job.
Calibration, in which the viewer follows dots so that the tracker learns his or her eyes, is part of every session (section 05).
A Welcome slide greets the viewer.
An Instructions slide gives the task in the same words to everyone: "Watch the screen as you would watch television at home."
It must not name the brand or the comparison, because a viewer who guesses what the researcher hopes to see tends to supply it, a demand effect.
Before each commercial comes a baseline, a neutral rest screen that lets each commercial start from the same calm state and, in Workshops 3 and 4, gives other sensors a resting level.
After each commercial comes a rating slide, a survey slide (a screen that asks a question) where the viewer rates liking from 1 to 7.
Two more decisions are written now.

The exclusion rule: a viewer whose Valid data (the percentage of expected gaze samples the tracker delivered) is below 70 percent is excluded, and every viewer's calibration result (Excellent, Good, or Poor) and recalibrations go into the session log.
Calibration and the viewer's eyes both affect data quality, and a rule chosen after seeing who looks bad is chosen to get a result.
Then the A O I master list: dynamic A O I's are drawn after collection but planned now from the storyboard, the shot by shot plan of the commercial.
The times below belong to the simulated plan, not to the real commercials.
Last, consent.

Informed consent is a documented explanation, given before participation, of the five items the iMotions consent F A Q lists: the purpose, that taking part is voluntary and can be withdrawn, the participant's rights, how the data will be handled, and the risks.
What a person looks at can reveal interests, health, and identity, and the face video of Workshop 3 identifies the viewer outright.
The N M S B A code of ethics sets out the participant rights that commercial studies should respect (Neuromarketing Science and Business Association, n.d.)
At Jacksonville State a study that will be published or presented first goes to the Institutional Review Board (I R B), the committee that reviews research with human participants.
Defend a counterbalanced within subjects design, explain d z and plan the sample, say what two stimuli can show, and fix the session, exclusion rule, A O I list, and consent in advance.
The worked example in full
Everything in sections 01 and 02 fits on one page, and writing that page is the first deliverable of any study in this lab.
Below is the commercial test as a student study plan, following the design of the simulated data set.
Read it as a template: change the commercials, the A O I's, and the numbers, and you have the plan for your own test.
Among adult viewers, which of two commercials for the same television brand, Balls or Paint, holds more attention on the product and on the brand at the end, and which is liked more?
H1: Dwell time ( percent) on Product TV is higher in Paint than in Balls.
H2: T T F F A O I (milliseconds) on Brand Logo is shorter in Paint.
H3: liking (1 to 7) differs between the commercials, two tailed.
Within subjects, one factor (commercial) with two levels.
Two flows for counterbalancing, Order A (Balls first) and Order B (Paint first), allocated alternately from a list prepared before collection; the order is stored as Group (A or B).
Commercial 1 Balls and Commercial 2 Paint, 60 seconds each in the simulation.
Welcome, Instructions, then for each commercial a Baseline slide, the commercial, and a rating slide.

Four dynamic A O I's with the active intervals planned in section 02: Product TV (14 seconds in Balls, 20 seconds in Paint), Brand Logo (last 5 seconds), Tagline Text (last 4 seconds), and Hero Element (40 seconds in Balls, 32 seconds in Paint).
The list is final before collection.
30 viewers scheduled (R 01 to R 30), 15 per order, for a target of at least 25 usable; 15 usable viewers give 80 percent power for d z equals 0.8.
"Watch the screen as you would watch television at home," read in the same words to every viewer.
Eye tracking, per viewer, commercial, and A O I: Dwell time ( percent), T T F F A O I (milliseconds), respondent ratio, fixation count, and revisit count.
Survey: liking of each commercial (1 to 7) on its rating slide; at the end, unaided brand recall (Yes or No) and the preferred commercial.
Exclude a viewer whose Valid data is below 70 percent.
Log every viewer's calibration result and recalibrations.
For each hypothesis, a two tailed paired t test on the Paint minus Balls differences, with d z and its 95 percent confidence interval, checked by a Wilcoxon signed rank test.
H2 on the viewers with a T T F F A O I value in both commercials, plus a sensitivity analysis for viewers who never fixated the logo.
A mixed model of Product TV dwell share with commercial, order position, their interaction, and a random intercept per viewer, to check the order effect.
Brand recall against logo dwell time with a point biserial correlation.
Alpha point 0 5.
An A O I table by commercial, heatmaps for named moments, three figures, a results section and a discussion in journal form, and a three sentence client summary.

Three names in the analysis plan return in section 08: the Wilcoxon signed rank test checks the paired t test using the ranks of the differences instead of their values; the mixed model is a regression that knows which rows come from the same viewer; the point biserial correlation relates a measurement to a yes or no answer.
Each hypothesis has one primary measure, and the pairing is the heart of the plan.

H1 uses Dwell time ( percent) on Product TV, a share rather than milliseconds, because the television set is on screen for 14 seconds in Balls and 20 in Paint; a share of the active time puts both on one scale.

H2 uses T T F F A O I (milliseconds) on Brand Logo, timed from the moment the logo appears, with the respondent ratio (the percentage of viewers who fixated the A O I at all) as a check that a faster time does not come from fewer viewers looking.
H3 uses the liking ratings, which no gaze metric can supply.
Brand recall and the preferred commercial are secondary measures of memory and affect, and Tagline Text and Hero Element are described, not tested.
The real material sits in the lab's Library.

"the demo Sony Bravia study" is a demonstration study from iMotions built around two Sony Bravia commercials from the "Colour like no other" campaign by the agency Fallon: "Balls" (2005), in which 250,000 rubber balls bounce down a San Francisco street, and "Paint" (2006), directed by Jonathan Glazer, filmed in Glasgow, and first aired in the United Kingdom on October 17, 2006.

Its stimuli are named Welcome, Instructions, Baseline1, Baseline1 Loading, Commercial1A Balls, Commercial1A Balls Loading, Commercial1A Balls Rating, Commercial1B Balls, Commercial1B Balls Loading, Commercial1B Balls Rating, Commercial2 Paint, Commercial2 Paint Loading, Commercial2 Paint Rating, Baseline2, Baseline2 Loading, Thank You, and Commercial1A Balls Frog, and its Recorded Data tab lists four respondents (iMotions' word for participants), R1 to R4.

The names echo the parts of the flow that section 04 builds: Welcome, Instructions, a Baseline, a commercial with its rating slide, a second Baseline, a second commercial with its rating slide, and a Thank You.

What the names do not tell you (the order in which the demo study plays them, how long each stimulus runs, which sensors recorded the respondents, why there are two Balls stimuli, what the Loading and Frog stimuli are) you find by opening the study on the lab laptop, not by guessing.
Wherever a number about viewers appears, it is simulated Four respondents are too few for any test, and this workshop reports no results from the demo study.
Every other number about viewers, in any section, comes from a simulated data set built to mirror a two commercial test of this kind.
No viewer was recorded for it, and none of its numbers may be quoted as a finding about the real commercials or real viewers.
The three simulated data files sit in the site's data folder.
One script, make simulated data dot P Y (seed 20268242), generated all three, and each opens with a line that says simulated.
SIMULATED ad test AOI metrics dot C S V is the file the statistics use: one row per respondent, commercial, and A O I, so 30 viewers, 2 commercials, and 4 A O I's give 240 rows.

The identifier columns say whose row it is: Study Name, Respondent Name (R 01 to R 30), Gender, Age, Group (the order, A or B, not a treatment), Session Date, Stimulus (Commercial 1 Balls or Commercial 2 Paint), and A O I Name.

The metric columns copy the names in the iMotions A O I Metrics article: Stimulus duration, A O I duration (milliseconds) and ( percent), Valid data, Gaze Hit time A O I (milliseconds), Gaze Dwell count, Gaze Dwell time (milliseconds), Dwells with fixations, Revisit count, Fixation count, T T F F A O I (milliseconds), T T F F parent (milliseconds), T T F F max.
(milliseconds), Dwell time (milliseconds), Dwell time ( percent), Fixation duration (milliseconds), and First fixation duration (milliseconds); section 06 defines each.

The manuals name these metrics but do not print the header row of a real export, so the header layout of a real Individual A O I metrics export has to be verified on the lab machine; the simulated file uses the manual's metric names without claiming to reproduce a real header row.
Where a viewer never fixated an A O I, the fixation based metrics read N A, which means not observed, not zero.
SIMULATED ad test survey dot C S V has one row per respondent: Liking Balls 1to7, Liking Paint 1to7, Brand recall (Yes or No), and Ad preferred.

SIMULATED ad test session log dot C S V is the operator's log: Respondent Name, Session Date, Operator, Group, Calibration result, Recalibrations, Distance to screen (cm), Glasses worn, Valid data ( percent), Data complete, and Decision note.
All three files share Respondent Name, which joins them.

One log row, R 23 in Group A, records Valid data of 58 percent and a calibration that stayed Poor after two recalibrations, with the decision exclude, which leaves 29 viewers, 14 in Group A and 15 in Group B (all simulated).
The folder also holds analysis.

R with its output (analysis output dot T X T) and the result tables it writes, the Excel workbook SIMULATED ad test analysis dot X L S X with its guide, and results text dot M D, the model paragraphs that sections 06, 09, and 10 adapt.
One deliverable is a picture rather than a number.
A heatmap lays color over the stimulus where viewers looked, transparent where nobody looked and red where attention gathered most.
The help center calls heatmaps purely qualitative visualizations: they show, and the A O I's supply the numbers.
On a commercial a heatmap belongs to a moment or an interval, never to the whole video at once; section 07 explains why.
Write the one page study plan, pair each hypothesis with its primary measure, describe the demo study from its stimulus names without guessing, and say which simulated file answers which question.
Building the study in iMotions Lab 11 point 1
The Study Builder turns the design from section 02 into the session a viewer will sit through; each screen asks a question the design has already answered.

If you did Workshop 1, notice the difference: a glasses study holds one stimulus, the recording, while a screen based study holds a flow, an ordered list of stimuli (the videos and slides shown on the screen).
Because every viewer sees both commercials (a within subjects design), the order is part of the design and is built into the study.
Either lab computer works, since both license keys include Eye Tracking Screen based.
Open the wizard.
Press control plus N or click the "+" next to Library.

You should see "Create a new study" with seven tiles: Screen-based, Remote Data Collection, Glasses, Screen-free recording, Mobile device, Smart Eye Pro, and Test Plan (confirmed on the lab laptop on October 7, 2026).
Common mistake.
Choosing Remote Data Collection, which sends a study to respondents online rather than to the lab monitor.
Choose Screen-based and click Next.
On the sensor page select Eye tracking and uncheck everything else; the Aurora itself is connected in Global Settings (section 05).
You should see Eye tracking as the only sensor; how the tile names the Aurora should be verified on the lab machine.
Common mistake.
Leaving an unused sensor checked.
Describe the respondent screen.
Pick the lab monitor from the presets, or enter its width and height in centimeters and its resolution, and save it.
Why: iMotions needs the physical size to calculate gaze angles.
The visual angle is the size of something as seen from the eye, in degrees, and depends on size and distance; the fixation filter and A O I padding in section 06 are stated in degrees.
Windows scaling distorts auto detection (a 1920 x 1080 monitor at 125 percent reads as 1536 x 864), and survey slides need Display Scaling at 100 percent, so set 100 percent first.
You should see the monitor's real size and native resolution.
Common mistake.
Accepting the laptop's own screen.
Name the study on the "Name your study" page by the lab convention year, client, topic (for example 2026 ClassPractice TwoCommercials) and finish the wizard.
You should see the study in the Library.
Common mistake.
Keeping the default timestamp name.

The flow is the session in order: Welcome, Instructions, a Baseline (a neutral rest screen before each commercial), the first commercial and its rating slide, a second Baseline, the second commercial and its rating slide, and a thank you.
The the demo Sony Bravia study study uses names such as Baseline1, Commercial1A Balls, and Commercial1A Balls Rating, which suggest the same pattern; open the study on the lab laptop to see its flow.
Open the builder.
Select your study and click Edit stimuli.
You should see the Flow designer tab (Study flows, Repository, and Properties panels; tiles for Block, Media, Survey, Screen recording, Website, and Qualtrics) and the Stimuli overview tab.
Common mistake.
Editing the demo study instead of your own.
Add the media.
Click Media and add the two commercials.
The manual prints the video formats as "MP4 or wave", probably a misprint, so play every video in the study preview.
If one lags, flickers, or has poor sound, right-click the study in the Library, choose "Convert videos for compatibility", and preview again.
You should see smooth playback.
Common mistake.
Expecting a new file type: the command replaces the original and does not change the format.
Add the rating slides.
Click Survey, add a Scale element for liking from 1 to 7, give it a Question I D that names the commercial (Liking Balls, Liking Paint), and click Save to Study.
A survey slide asks a question on screen; the Question I D labels the answer in the survey results.
Do not randomize questions or labels, which ties all video replays to one image.
You should see the slide in the flow.
Common mistake.
Two slides with the same Question I D.
Group and fix the order.
Select a commercial and its rating slide and press control plus G to make a block, a group of stimuli that moves as a unit: Block Balls and Block Paint.
The pin icon fixes a stimulus in place and the arrow icon randomizes it, so pin both.
Baseline1 and Baseline2 are separate stimuli because a stimulus cannot appear twice in one flow.
You should see Welcome, Instructions, Baseline1, Block Balls, Baseline2, Block Paint, Thank You.
Common mistake.
An arrow left on a rating slide, which can show the rating first.
Set the properties.

Select several stimuli to edit them together, then check the Stimuli overview tab: presentation duration and display order for each, the same duration for both Baselines, and manual advance for the rating slides.
Common mistake.
A rating slide that advances before the viewer answers.
Why: the second commercial carries practice, fatigue, and comparison with the first.
Counterbalancing shows half the viewers each order, so these order effects cancel out of the comparison.
Duplicate the flow.
In the Study flows panel click Duplicate flow (Add flow starts an empty one) and, in the copy, swap Block Balls and Block Paint: Order A shows Balls first, Order B Paint first.
You should see two flows with the same stimuli in different orders.
Flows share stimulus properties (a duration changed in one changes in both), but each keeps its own order.
Common mistake.
Moving a commercial without its rating slide; move whole blocks.
Choose the allocation.
On Study Settings choose manual selection or randomization by iMotions.
This workshop selects manually from a list written in advance (A, B, A, B), which keeps the groups equal.
Common mistake.
Not logging each viewer's order, which makes the order effect untestable in section 08.

A test plan, created through the Test Plan tile from a C S V of respondents (NAME, GENDER, AGE, CITY) and a Stimuli folder, is the alternative for many versions; for two orders, two flows are simpler.

The Aurora and the session
The Aurora is a bar under the monitor that lights the eyes with infrared light and films them.

Its software finds the pupil center and the reflection of the light on the cornea (the clear front of the eye) and computes where the eye points, a method called pupil center corneal reflection (P C C R).
The lab's unit records 60 gaze samples (estimated gaze points) per second, one every 16.67 milliseconds; that is its sampling rate (Smart Eye, n.d.)
Unlike the Neon in Workshop 1, it must be told where the screen is and must learn each viewer's eyes.
Why: the tracker measures the eyes relative to itself, and a setup tells it where it sits on the screen.
A new setup is required "if Windows Display Settings are changed or a different eye tracker model is used", so a new monitor or scaling value means a new setup.

From gaze samples to metrics: what a 60 hertz screen based tracker measures, and how to describe it

Every number in the results ends a chain: the Aurora records gaze samples, a filter sorts them into fixations and saccades, dynamic areas of interest mark where and when each element is on screen, and A O I metrics summarize what landed inside.
The reporting standards ask for the apparatus, the processing, and the exclusion rules, and the handbooks supply the vocabulary.
The Aurora lights the eyes with infrared light and locates the pupil and the corneal reflection, the pupil center corneal reflection principle.
Each estimate of where the viewer looks is one gaze sample.
At the lab unit's sampling rate of 60 hertz (Smart Eye, n.d.)

, a sample arrives every 16.67 milliseconds, so a 60 seconds commercial yields about 3,600 samples per viewer and a 100 milliseconds fixation, the short end of the typical 100 to 300 milliseconds range, spans about six.
If you did Workshop 1, note that a fixed screen needs no gaze mapping: every viewer sees the same frame at the same moment.
In plain words.
Accuracy: does the tracker point to the right place?
Gaze recorded a centimeter left of the dot a viewer stares at is inaccurate, even if every sample lands on one spot.
Precision: does it point to the same place twice?
Samples scattered around the dot are imprecise, even if their average is on target.

The definitions in the literatureAccuracy is the average offset between measured and true gaze position, in degrees of visual angle.

The iMotions manuals define neither term.
Both suffer with a poor calibration, glasses, contact lenses, and some eye physiology, and with head movement and a poor seating distance.

iMotions reports a calibration label (Excellent, Good, or Poor) and Valid data, the percentage of collected and interpolated samples, neither an accuracy in degrees; whether the Smart Eye software reports one must be verified on the lab machine.
A fixation is a period in which the eyes rest on one location long enough to take in detail; a saccade is the fast jump between fixations.
Researchers disagree on the definitions (Hessels and colleagues
, 2018), so a methods section gives an operational one: whatever the named filter, with its listed parameters, classified as a fixation.
Filters threshold velocity or dispersion.
The lab uses I V T, velocity threshold identification: samples slower than the threshold form fixations, faster ones saccades.
Velocity is measured in degrees of visual angle per second, an angle that depends on the distance to the screen, which is why the I V T article calls the screen parameters "absolutely crucial."

The study's Gaze Analysis tab holds Window Length, Velocity Threshold, Gap Fill-in with Max Gap Length, Noise Reduction (which can remove signal at low sampling rates), Discard Short Fixations with Minimum Fixation Duration, and Merge Adjacent Fixations.
The article states no defaults and calls I V T "typically used for higher-sampling eye tracking data (200 hertz or more)," with no rule for 60 hertz.
So report the filter and every parameter exactly as the tab shows them, use the same settings for every respondent, and never interpret a single short fixation.

Gaze smoothing, a tick box in the Visualization menu (named Visualizations in the Gaze smoothing article; verify on the lab machine) that averages the drawn gaze over 160 milliseconds (about 9 or 10 samples), is "exclusively for visualization purposes" and never changes fixations or exports.
An area of interest (A O I) is a region whose gaze iMotions summarizes.
Commercial elements move and come and go, so the A O I's are dynamic, with active intervals on a timeline and key frames that move the shape with the element.

The A O I master list fixes them in advance: in the simulated design Product TV is active 14 seconds in Balls and 20 seconds in Paint, Brand Logo the last 5 seconds, Tagline Text the last 4 seconds, and Hero Element 40 seconds and 32 seconds respectively.
A tight shape misses real looks and a loose one catches the neighbors', the trade that treating A O I's as a signal detection problem makes explicit (Orquin and colleagues
, 2016); the Areas of Interest article suggests padding of about 1 to 1.5 degrees, roughly 1 to 2 cm at 60 cm.
For a small logo, a fixation counts as inside if one of its samples is, and a dwell begins only after the dwell classification threshold, 100 milliseconds by default.
In the A O I Metrics article, "parent" means the stimulus holding the A O I, here the commercial.
Time to first fixation (T T F F) has three versions.
"How quickly after the logo appeared did viewers fixate it?"
needs a clock that starts with the end card, so H2 uses T T F F A O I; T T F F parent would add the 55 seconds before the end card to every value.
T T F F max.
keeps viewers who never noticed the logo by treating never as the end of the commercial; the five never fixated rows in the simulated file carry 60,000 milliseconds.
iMotions writes N A when a metric cannot be calculated; an N A in T T F F means not observed, never zero.

With no real difference, these would average about zero.
The paired t test asks whether the average difference is far from zero relative to how much the differences vary.

The same test in symbols t equals Md / (standard deviation of the differences / the square root of n), df equals n minus 1; d z equals Md divided by standard deviation of the differences, so t equals d z × the square root of n Simulated H1: Md equals 7.25 percentage points (Paint minus Balls), standard deviation of the differences equals 7.40, n equals 29, so t(28) equals 5.27, p less than point 0 0 1; 95 percent confidence interval of the difference 4.43 to 10.06.

If you did Workshop 1, you used Welch's test, which compares two independent groups; here both columns come from the same 29 people in a within subjects design, and a viewer's two dwell shares correlate, r equals point 4 8 (simulated).
The paired test removes that shared part from the error, the source of its power.
In Excel it is one argument: T dot test type 1 (paired) instead of type 3.
The effect size for a paired test is d z, the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of the differences.

For H1, d z equals 0.98 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.53 to 1.42 from the noncentral t distribution, a large effect by the usual labels; Paint was higher for 25 of 29 viewers (simulated).

Exercises: from two commercials to a pilot protocol
Five exercises that take you through the arc yourself.

Exercise 1 asks you to write the comparison sentence and three hypotheses for a two commercial test of a product you choose; Exercise 2 is the sample size calculation for a paired test, compared with a between subjects design; Exercise 3 rebuilds the R analysis of the simulated data one step at a time; Exercise 4 does the paired test for H1 in Excel; and Exercise 5 is the practical, a two person pilot on the lab monitor with the Aurora, written as a protocol with two flows, the calibration routine, the session log, and the A O I master list.

Each exercise gives a hint, then a "Build it" game in which you pick the right line (code or a formula in Exercises 3 and 4, the right statement in 1, 2, and 5), then a walkthrough, then a full model solution with a copy button.
Every number printed in the games is simulated and comes from analysis output dot T X T or the Excel walkthrough.
